problem: Existing VLN benchmarks use think-out-loud instructions written while viewing the environment, in house or street navigation graphs. They do not capture memory-based route instructions from sighted passersby (with errors, omissions and stutters) in large maze-like public spaces where blind users navigate.
motivation: Robots guiding blind people could rely on sighted passersby's verbal directions in unfamiliar buildings without prebuilt maps. Such directions come from human memory and contain distance errors, hallucinated landmarks and missing turns, so a benchmark reflecting this is needed to test whether current VLN models cope.
key_idea: Build Memory-Maze, a CARLA-based benchmark of real public-space replicas with both online think-out-loud and onsite memory-based route instructions, plus a zero-shot single-inference LLM code-generation baseline with modular navigation APIs.
insight: Memory-based onsite instructions are longer, more lexically diverse and have far higher failure rates (e.g. 25-76% vs 0-18%) than online ones, and model performance is generally lower on them. Even a baseline with privileged modular perception/control gets near-zero SR on long routes, so the bottleneck is language interpretation and reasoning under errors and topological ambiguity (e.g. 'go along this path'). The instruction parser generally helps (Table 2), while refining instructions helps only slightly and sometimes hurts because of redundant object descriptions.
method: CARLA environment: Fusion 360 3D replicas of a university floor and two museum floors (3 environments, 6 routes) with RGB, depth and LiDAR sensors and static/dynamic obstacles.

Control API: move_forward(distance) with PID center-corridor tracking, detect_turning_point() using pre-annotated areas, turn(direction), and detect_from_RGB_image(object) via Grounding DINO with tracking and a 4 m depth filter.

Instruction data: online study (78 participants, 312 instructions from walkthrough videos, translated with GPT-4) and onsite in-person memory study (83 participants, 252 instructions), each with two iterations (natural, then after robot capability explanation and error pointing).
Instruction parser: GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) converts the instruction into step-by-step itemized sentences via two-stage thought/refine prompting.
Code generator: GPT-4 with the API spec and docstrings generates Python navigation code in one inference (two-stage prompting), executed with the API implementation without a navigation graph.
Metrics: SR, OSR, SPD, and CLS computed on a 50 cm grid graph; the described route is used as ground truth for alternative routes.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview, frozen) with Grounding DINO; baselines NavGPT (GPT-4o-mini) and NaVid (Vicuna-7B)
setting.training_data: none (training-free; prompt built from 5 online-study instructions)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth (simulated), with LiDAR available
setting.action_space: high-level API calls (move_forward, turn, detect_turning_point, detect object) with PID low-level control
setting.privileged: corridor corner coordinates and turning-point areas taken from the simulator; initial robot orientation given

numbers.extra: privileged corridor/turning-point geometry; single-inference code generation

numbers_note: Results are given per route (6 routes x online/onsite) with SR as fractions (0-1); only a few representative rows are listed. Other routes are in Table 2, and iteration-wise results in Table 3. There is no official split, so 'test' is used for the benchmark.
results: The proposed zero-shot code-generation baseline outperforms NavGPT and NaVid, which get about 0 SR on nearly all routes (e.g. University R1: SR 0.04 and 0.00 vs 0.30 with parser). Performance on onsite memory-based instructions is generally lower than on online ones, but even the best model has very low SR on long routes.
limitations: Small benchmark, too limited for training; only three environments and six routes, with online instructions translated by GPT-4 from Japanese.
Baseline uses privileged simulator geometry (corridor corners, turning-point areas) and open-loop single-shot code generation without closed-loop verification.
Real-world robot deployment is not evaluated; NavGPT and NaVid are applied outside their training distribution.
